newsitem.title: FRANCE: France extends bank opening to six-day week.
newsitem.headline: France extends bank opening to six-day week.

text.p: The French government, ditching a 60-year-old system obliging banks to close on weekends, adopted a decree on Wednesday to allow bank branches stay open six days a week and for a longer time each day.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said a new decree adopted at a cabinet meeting would allow six-day opening and banks would now also be able to open from 7.30 in the morning to 8.30 at night, doing away with the current eight-hour day limit.
The new regulatory system replaces one in place since 1937.
Arthuis said the change could help to protect employment in the sector and that it marked an important step in the reform of the financial and banking system.
"It is in line with the interests of the client, it is in line with the interests of staff. Also we will be able to save 10,000 jobs," he told reporters after the cabinet meeting.

Unions have attacked the way the government has gone about the reform and are threatening to step up their protests after a once-day strike last week which drew a modest following. There were warnings on Tuesday that their action could go as far as seeking to snarl traffic on highways or block railway tracks.

Arthuis said more flexible hours would pave the way for reductions in working time in certain cases. Sunday will remain a rest day under the new decree and staff will still have the right to a two-day break per week.
Some French banks have been able to open on Saturday because of their special status but the aim is to extend this to commercial banks which have been unable to do so.
